function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into a terminal (or run in a CI job) to finish the task.  
I’ve broken it into the four numbered steps you listed, and added a few extra notes for clarity.

> **⚠️ Important** – All commands assume you’re running them from the root of a fresh clone of the repository (or that you have a working copy of `nodejs-welcome` locally).  
> If you’re on Windows, replace `git`, `bash`, and `sed` with their PowerShell equivalents or use WSL.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1.1  Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you don’t have SSH access, use the HTTPS URL instead:
> ```bash
> git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
> cd nodejs-welcome
> ```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Analyse the repository

We’ll use the `analyse_repo_contents` helper to get a quick overview of the dominant language(s).  
(If you’re running this locally, you can skip the function call and just eyeball the repo.)

```bash
# 2.1.1  Analyse repo (optional – just for reference)
# (This step is only needed if you want to programmatically decide on Dockerfile/K8s settings.)
# You can run it in a Python REPL or a small script:

python - <<'PY'
from functions import analyse_repo_contents
print(analyse_repo_contents(
    directory_name=".",          # current dir
    include_subdirectories=True,
    excluded_files=["README.md"],
    language_threshold=10.0
))
PY
```

> The output will look something like:
> ```json
> {"language":"JavaScript","percentage":95.3}
> ```

### 2.2 Create / update the Dockerfile

```bash
# 2.2.1  Generate Dockerfile
# (If you prefer to hand‑write it, you can skip this step and create a Dockerfile manually.)
# Using the helper function:
python - <<'PY'
from functions import create_a_docker_file
create_a_docker_file(
    directory_name=".",
    base_image="node:18-alpine",
    maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>",
    port=3000,
    commands="npm ci; npm run build"
)
PY
```

> If you prefer to write it yourself, a minimal Dockerfile for this repo would be:

```Dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set maintainer
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

# Copy source
COPY . .

# Build (if you have a build step)
RUN npm run build

# Expose port
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

```bash
# 2.3.1  Generate K8s YAML
python - <<'PY'
from functions import create_kubernetes_yaml_file
create_kubernetes_yaml_file(
    directory_name=".",
    deployment_name="nodejs-welcome",
    image_name="zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest",
    replicas=3,
    service_type="ClusterIP",
    port=80,
    target_port=3000
)
PY
```

> The helper will create a file named `k8s.yaml` (or similar) containing both a Deployment and a Service.  
> If you’d rather hand‑write it, here’s a quick template:

```yaml
# k8s.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest .
          docker login ghcr.io -u ${{ github.actor }} -p ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          docker tag zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Tip:** If you want to push to Docker Hub instead of GitHub Container Registry, replace the `docker login` and `docker push` lines accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage all changes

```bash
# 3.1  Add all new/modified files
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

> If you used the helper functions, they already created the files in the repo root.  
> If you hand‑wrote any of them, just make sure they’re staged.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
# 4.1  Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"

# 4.2  Push to remote
git push origin main
```

> If you’re on a protected branch that requires a PR, you can push to a new branch and open a PR instead:

```bash
git checkout -b add-docker-k8s-ci
git push -u origin add-docker-k8s-ci
# Then open a PR on GitHub
```

---

### 🎉 Done!

You now have:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a container image for the Node.js app |
| `k8s.yaml` | Deployment + Service for Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | GitHub Actions pipeline that builds & pushes the image on every push to `main` |

Feel free to tweak the Docker image tag, number of replicas, or CI steps to match your organization’s conventions. Happy coding!
